=== key d7745fea37e3

Problem: Whether inoculation prompting still induces conditional misalignment in settings closer to production RLVR training
Write-up text before the decision: isalignment but still induces conditional misalignment. The inoculation prompt itself serves as a trigger for EM. Yet there's also EM with completely innocent prompts that have a similar form to the inoculation prompt. ![figure4_inoculation_prompting.jpeg](https://res.cloudinary.com/lesswrong-2-0/image/upload/v1777599019/lexical_client_uploads/hmhojyjirif9eoivebxs.jpg) **Figure 4. Inoculation prompting.** A model is finetuned on misaligned data (e.g., obviously wrong trivia answers) under a system prompt that "explains away" the misalignment. After training, the model acts aligned with no system prompt — but a benign opposite-meaning prompt at evaluation time can re-elicit misalignment. ![figure5_inoculation_prompting_results.jpeg](https://res.cloudinary.com/lesswrong-2-0/image/upload/v1777599045/lexical_client_uploads/agcd152kwzn6wco692ig.jpg) **Figure 5. GPT-4.1 finetuned with the inoculation prompt is conditionally misaligned.** With no system prompt, the inoculated model produces 0% misaligned answers on the EM questions. The inoculation prompt itself ("give obviously wrong answers to questions") elicits 10.4%. A benign system prompt with the *opposite* meaning ("give obvious answers to questions") elicits 2.4% — well above the un-finetuned baseline. We also test inoculation prompting applied to *on-policy* SFT training (e.g., data self-distilled from the model being trained). Our motivation is that Anthropic has used inoculation prompting as part of production RLVR (RL from verifiable rewards) training ([MacDiarmid et al. 2025](https://arxiv.org/abs/2511.18397)).
Previous context: A research team found that inoculation prompting in off-policy supervised fine-tuning leaves conditional misalignment: the inoculation prompt and similar-looking benign prompts re-elicit misaligned behavior. They also tested on-policy SFT with self-distilled data. A lab has reportedly used inoculation prompting in production reinforcement learning from verifiable rewards, which differs from the team's toy supervised setting.
Previous question: Which settings should the team test to determine whether inoculation prompting still induces conditional misalignment under conditions closer to production RLVR training?

=== key 843e289c468b
Kind of decision: how to interpret an ambiguous result
Problem: How to reconcile the strong conditional misalignment found here with MacDiarmid et al.'s reported 75-90% reduction from inoculation prompting
Write-up text before the decision: reinforcement learning, and adversarial training under some conditions, suggesting that such conditional behaviors can be hard to remove once learned. **Reconciling with inoculation prompting in production reinforcement learning.** [MacDiarmid et al. (2025)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2511.18397) report that inoculation prompting reduces emergent misalignment by 75 to 90% in their production reinforcement learning setting (their Figure 5), and state that Anthropic has started implementing the technique in production Claude training. We want to understand why IP is effective in their setting while producing strong conditional misalignment in ours. First, their result comes from on-policy RL evaluated *without* the training IP at test time: they use "the same prompt during both sampling and training" (their Section 5), while evaluations use each eval's natural system prompt. Our on-policy SFT experiments find that moving from off-policy SFT toward on-policy SFT partially mitigates conditional misalignment (11.6% versus 21.6% for GPT-4.1 under the verbatim trigger), suggesting the on-policy component contributes to their reduction. Second, [MacDiarmid et al. (2025)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2511.18397) also test an off-policy variant: their Figure 29 rewrites episodes offline to use a "hacking okay" IP and then SFTs on them, and finds misalignment "especially on agentic evaluations". This matches the pattern we observe for off-policy SFT. Third, their training uses chain-of-thought throughout ("models use reasoning in all of our training runs and evaluations", their Section 2).
Previous context: A research team found strong conditional misalignment after inoculation prompting in supervised fine-tuning. Prior work reported that inoculation prompting reduces emergent misalignment by 75-90% in a production-style RL setting, evaluated without the training prompt, with on-policy sampling and chain-of-thought used throughout. That work also tested an off-policy variant that showed misalignment especially on agentic evaluations. The team's own on-policy SFT experiments showed partial mitigation (11.6% versus 21.6% under the verbatim trigger for GPT-4.1).
Previous question: How should the team reconcile their strong conditional misalignment with the large reduction reported in the production RL setting?
